sections.content:
This is a non-cumulative course. The content itself is fairly trivial, though you do need good calculator skills. In my opinion, it is much, much easier than ECON 2123.

Process Analysis & Capacity
Capacity Planning
Resource Allocation
Service & Queuing Models
Quality Management & Statistical Process Control

Forecasting
Inventory Management & Newsvendor Model
Revenue Management
Supply Chain Management
Just-in-Time Production
sections.teaching: The professor has an incredibly thick accent. To make matters worse, despite her highly unclear teaching, she also chooses not to release lecture recordings. The lecture slides are equally poorly made—I mean, why on earth is the main text color RED? She seriously needs to learn how to annotate her slides properly.
sections.grading:
--- Grading Scheme ---
20% In-class Quizzes (ABSOLUTELY HORRIBLE)
40% Midterm Exam
40% Final Exam
--- Statistics --- (Mean, SD, Me)
Midterm Exam: 67.8, 17.2, 94
Final Exam: 67.7, 17.7, 92

I managed to get full marks on the in-class quizzes, but the process was agonizing. Because of "skill issues" (frequently getting 4/5 on those iPRS quizzes), I was forced to attend almost every single lecture just to gamble for pop quiz points to make up for it. I hated this.

Final Grade: A+
sections.workload:
Absolutely ZERO workload. I spent one day revising for the midterm and two days for the final, which turned out to be more than enough. There is no homework or after-class tasks, so it honestly feels like this should be a 2-credit course instead.

A great way to study for this course is to feed all your materials into NotebookLM. That's what I did—asking it to generate mock exam papers was incredibly useful.

Definitely take this course if you want a light workload and decent grading.

sections.teaching: Personally, I liked his teaching very much. He goes at a very adequate speed, focuses on the most important topics during lectures, and always tries to communicate with the class. So, if you pay attention and ask him questions during class, it will definitely be helpful for you. He also has these 5-minute breaks in the middle of a class, where you can walk up to him and ask questions one-on-one, in case you're uncomfortable with speaking to the whole class.

Operations management is about designing, analyzing, and improving the whole transformation process, including procurement, production, distribution, warehousing, and retailing, with the objective of creating competitive advantage for the enterprise.
ISOM 2700 is designated as a face-to-face learning course and you are expected to review the learning materials on Canvas before attending the student-centered instructor-led session every week. You are encouraged to use AI tools appropriately to enhance your learning.

I write this review because I saw most of the other reviews are saying that it is a good course so I want to provide mine as an example of the opposite. This course is inevitable for me as it is a business core but for those interested think carefully if you really want to study this course.

sections.teaching:
I am not here to go through the syllabus but am here to document my journey to getting a nice grade in this course.

First of all, reg Professor Shen, I am from pathway 2 but I registered in spring because Prof Shen only teaches Spring.

Second, listen to his lectures. Although the slides are very concise and self-contained, which are user-friendly for self-study, Prof Shen walks you through what’s important and what the intuition is behind everything, it really helps build our business acumen, especially when we can always see “trade offs” in different chapters, which is the essence of optimisation.

In fact, for the exam questions, about 75% are calculation-based but 25% are conceptual, which has no calculations and requires us to discuss the directional impact of one variable on another, or ask us to clarify some concepts (eg. Profit and service level in newsvendor model; lead time and optimal ordering quantity in EOQ model; agility and adaptability in supply chain management). Professor says it is usually the questions without calculations that most people get it wrong, and the best way to deal with this is to listen to lectures, mark them down and write the exact statements on the cheatsheet so you can refer to it.

Thirdly, finish all practice questions. Professor provides: quizzes, HW, problem sets after each 2 lectures, and an extra problem set for each exam. I suggest doing all of them or at least reading through all the solutions, because there will be variations in some subtle things in the problem set ups, and I think Professor has encapsulated all possibilities that he could play with the concepts. Also, there are some non-calculation based questions which are exactly what I mentioned to be the questions with the lowest correct answering rate, and some of those exactly appear in the exam, which is why after finishing everything, I didn’t even have one question that I felt unsure when I took the mid term and finals.

Another thing is that professor has a review session that contains all the PowerPoint slides throughout the semester, but he actually selects what is tested and what is not, to minimise our load for revision. And when you studied the course you will know which page will be exactly tested and you can simply put the whole page into the cheat sheet. (For the finals, I managed to include 10 questions that are exactly asked)

The last crazy thing about Professor Shen, he replies emails as if he’s replying to WhatSapps. The average speed of reply is 30minutes to 1 hour. The slowest was the next day, but it was a Sunday morning. The fastest was in 2 minutes. I was shocked. You can basically ask him everything and he will always answer you in a structured way, sometimes using materials beyond the scope to give you a full picture and let you know what is to be tested and what assumptions are made to make the course simpler.

I just cannot say anything bad about Professor Shen.
He is in my top 3.

The assignments themselves are insanely easy (and a little boring), you basically have to replicate Suri's working in MS excel into your own excel sheet and submit it (no knowledge required on your part). For the midterm and the final if you go through all the lectures just once before the exam and make sure you know how to solve the problems included in the slides, you should be able to score an A (feel free to study more though!).

sections.content:
I find this class completely useless. You can refer to the other sections of what this class is about, basically complicated math that (in my humble opinion) I think has no applicability in real life. One of those courses where you will never use the stuff you learnt again in real life.

For example, you will learn how to "optimise" inventory and "optimal order quantity" with some complicated formula. But, WHY does this matter to us "business" students, a point of a business is to generate revenue, and what we learn has no correlation to generate revenue at all. It doesn't matter if you are a master at managing inventory when no one buys - and this is the struggle of most business and for us business students.

That being said, if you work for a global business like Mcdonalds, then yeah maybe you need to use those complex formulas to know how many burgers to make. But if the professor said that nowadays most inventory can be managed via computer systems or AI, so why are we learning this...

sections.teaching:
At the beginning of this semester when I was enrolled into his session, I was a bit nervous as I checked there was only little info about him here. So now I am here to tell you more about this super nice professor!

Prof Shen is extremely responsive and polite. He is super willing to respond to our enquires and questions. One thing that shocked me the most is that I am able to get his response via email within 20 mins every time.

Meanwhile, he puts a huge effort in teaching. You could definitely feel his passion if you were his students. His PPT is clear and to-the-point which is easy for me to comprehend. He also controls the pace of his teaching well. More on that, his pronunciation is clear and he is good at explaining concepts. Stupid people like me are able to understand what’s going on during the lecture. One thing that I love the most is that he will finish one PPT per lecture, and never splitting one PPT between 2 lectures. So every lecture will always start with a new topic. It is extremely friendly for students like me who will never revisit the learnt material after class:). However, no attendance is taken in his lesson and lecture recordings are uploaded on canvas punctually. Around 70% of students skipped his lesson. It is sad to see as Prof Shen really prepared a lot for his lecture.

In order to help us to prepare well for the exams, he posts a lot of practice questions of every chapter on Canvas and the question type is similar to what appeared in the exam.

Note: Every Monday he will hold a one hour consultation session online for us to ask questions.

He is a humble person who always ask for feedback about his lesson. (He really listened what we said and made improvement!!!)

The TA Jing is also very responsive and polite. In paper checking session, she will explain to us EVERY question that we got wrong in detail, even if I didn’t ask her. I saw her spending 45 mins explaining concepts to a student during the paper checking session.

However, this is another CC course where they don't allow you to appeal the scores you get in the examinations, or the final grade. "We have checked the answer and error rate for each exam question thoroughly and didn't find any major issue. sections.grading:
Online Quizzes (5+1): 20%
-Each online quiz consists of 10 questions.
-Once you start the quiz, the timer will start automatically and you must complete it within the time limit.
-The quiz with the lowest grade will be dropped, i.e., your quiz’s grade will be based on 5 quizzes.

Midterm Exam: 40%
Final Exam: 40%
-Midterm and final exam consist of 50 multiple choice questions and last 2 hours each.
- If you miss the midterm exam for a valid and verifiable reason approved by the instructor in advance, you will have to take a 3-hour, 80-question cumulative final exam (covering the entire course) and the weight of the mid-term will be added to the final exam. Otherwise, a zero mark will be assigned as your mid-term grade.
-Both exams are close-note and close-book

sections.workload: NO assignments and the only thing we have to do is the online quizzes. Professor will provide the problem sets(Not compulsory) for your learning purpose.

sections.content: The content is very interesting and seems useful. It is much more conceptual rather than mathematical unlike what I have heard about other ISOM courses. The math/statistics used in this course is very basic and the course tests your concepts rather than anything else.
sections.teaching: Teaching was absolutely phenomenal. Suri takes his time and teaches concepts clearly and you can relax in class and still understand everything he teaches. He's the only lecturer whose courses I actually attended since I enjoyed them. He requires you to turn on your camera during Wednesday lectures so that he can get an understanding of how the class is responding to his teaching.
sections.grading:
The grading was pretty good however the difference between the grade boundaries for an A and an A+ were quite close together. 90% for an A. 93% for an A+. I had a 91% and received an A.

20% was for Class participation & Quizzes. I received full in all quizzes besides one in which I received a 0.8/2 and still got the full 20 marks in class participation and quizzes.

35% was for Midterm and 45% for Final. Midterm and Final are non-cumulative so only topics completed after the midterm are tested in the final.
sections.workload: The workload is very less. One quiz/excel spreadsheet every week. In the beginning, there are some very simple 'quizzes' with a handful of questions and you get 2 attempts that you can attempt whenever you want with the camera off, etc. After the first 2 or so weeks, he uploads 30-45 minute video tutorials of him solving problems using excel spreadsheets and you simply have to follow along and upload the spreadsheet.

sections.content: The content for this course is mostly concept-based, strong math skills or knowledge is not necessary as the formula is provided. Although attedence is required, even if you miss his lectures, you can still look for the course materials in Canvas modules that the content is almost equivalent to a textbook, so don't worry if you missed his lectures.
sections.teaching: His teaching is very good. Unlike other professors, he will provide lots of example for the content he teaches, making it easy to understand and relatable for us. Also, the videos to show how to calculate the maths is really useful as it demonstrates how you would do that in the future when you are working.
sections.grading: Grade has not been released yet, but you do have to revise for the midterm/ final as most of them are conceptual questions that will require you to recall the knowledge and concepts learnt in the powerpoint and his Canvas materials, which neither cheet sheet or notes is allowed in the exams, but most of the equations will be provided.
sections.workload: Extremely light workload, just watch and complete an Excel spreadsheet per 1 or 2 weeks, no additional assignment or projects required.

This course just has a little touch on each topic. The content is quite different from some other courses which you may probably took beforehand like the ISOM2500 and ISOM2010. This course talks about statistics for very tiny part and do not talk about programming and coding. Therefore, you can expect this a brand new course for you even though it is a ISOM2000-level course.
sections.teaching: Professor Shin is a good teacher in a way that every concept in this course is explained thoroughly. Whenever you have questions, you can simply shoot them out, and he will answer you right away. He is also an expert in the revenue management part. Great speed of delivery.
sections.grading:
The content is quite easy and the after-class quiz is important for you to be outstanding.

After-class quizzes 20% (best 5 out of 6)
Midterm exam 40%
Final exam 40% (Non-cumulative, things in midterm will not be tested)

The after-class quizzes mainly focus on conceptual questions instead of numerical questions although most of the questions in midterm or final exam are going to be numerical questions. Take the conceptual question in easier mindset. You can answer those questions with some real life experience.

The difficulties for the numerical questions are not based on the mathematics itself. The difficulties are that you have to find the suitable equations to plug in all the numbers. Once you find that equations, they are easy.
sections.workload: Light. As there are only 3 things that account for the grade. You use fair hours of time to revise Midterm and Final exam. The after-class quiz is easy, and you can finish them in 10mins given that you will have 20mins for each quiz.

sections.content:
This semester is conducted online.

Part A: Managing Business Process Flow
Part B: Synchronizing Supply and Demand

Most content in part B overlaps with IEDA2200 (forecasting, inventory management, newsboy model, etc). You might as well take these two courses together, you can definitely recognize the similarity between these two.

Concepts are easy to understand, but when you actually work on those MCs in quizzes or exams, you might be very frustrated. Most questions (both qualitative and quantitative) are very confusing, and you don't know which variable it is talking about. I still don't know what was happening in those exams. Point is Ronald explicitly said he would make the exams less confusing, but no bitch he didn't.

sections.content:
This course teaches introductory operations management theories and methods. It gives nice insights to students as most of them are new to OM. The course is somehow like ISOM2500, but more concepts are included apart from calculation only.

Week 3: Capacity Planning
Week 4: Resource Optimization
Week 5: Managing Waiting Lines
Week 6: Managing Process Performance Variability
Week 8: Demand Management and Forecasting
Week 9: Inventory Management

Week 11: Revenue Management
Week 12: Supply Chain Management

I think the content is broad and deep enough for you to understand more about OM, and it really can raise your interest in OM.
I would say ISOM2700 is actually one of the best business introduction courses.

His online lectures are super useful as he will provide more details and skills for a certain concept or calculation. Make sure you study all online lectures if you are in his class. There is some extra information which is not included in class lectures.

Overall speaking, his teaching is good except he always updates his powerpoint few minutes before the start of the lesson and seldom explained much for some difficult concepts but using a lot of time to explain some simple common sense.

sections.content:
This introductory course will equip you (tomorrow’s managers) with an understanding of the concepts and tools necessary to make business (organizational) processes more “efficient”. Examples of such processes include auto manufacturing process, servicing customers in restaurants/coffee shops, healthcare services offered by hospitals, online marketplaces, sharing-economy platforms or airlines offering connections between different cities. These businesses/organizations are primarily concerned about: (1) creating value through products/services, which in turn generates demand; and (2) satisfying the demand in an “efficient’’ fashion. In this course, we will address the latter issue in a systematic fashion.  

(course description from SPRING 2018 course syllabus)

內容其實幾有趣，會有少少數 不過係普通logic野黎

1. Process Analysis and Improvement
Productivity & Operations Measures; Process Flowchart & Process Analysis; Process Types & Layouts, Assembly Line Balancing
2. Service Management
Variability, Utilization & Queuing; Queuing Models; Psychology of Waiting; Service Management
3. Capacity Management
Measuring Capacity and Concepts for Capacity Planning; Decision Tree Method; Linear Programming & Sensitivity Analysis
4. Inventory Management
Concepts for Managing Inventory; Newsboy Model; EOQ, Continuous Review Models; Cycle Counting & Practical Issues
5. Demand Management
Methods for Forecasting, Measuring Forecast Accuracy; Application of Newsboy Model in Price Differentiation & Overbooking
6. Quality Management
Concepts of Quality, TQM; Acceptance Sampling; Process Control; Process Capability Index & Six Sigma Quality
7. Supply Chain Strategies
Products vs. Supply Processes, Bullwhip Effect; Innovation through Supply Chains; Supply Chain Architecture; Sourcing Decision

sections.content:
The content has two main parts - operations management (before midterm), and supply chain management (after midterm).

Key topics include: capacity/bottleneck management, best practices, news-vendor model, supply chain strategies, revenue management, business model innovation.

Unlike the other professors (I think), Prof Cui's course is based more on case studies so it's really useful to read these as you can get a better understanding of the lecture materials taught.

Although there's a suggested textbook, it's not compulsory as all the content for the exams can be found in the case studies and lecture slides. That being said, the textbook has a lot of practice problems for the news-vendor model and capacity management topics, so it's useful to do these as practice for the final exam.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Cui is really passionate and enthusiastic about teaching during lectures, and this is reflected directly in how he interacts with students. He is really helpful and it's very easy to approach him and ask him questions about the course content or your group project (our group sent him a draft version of our report and he helped us a lot with it).

He tries his best to keep the lectures interesting, and gives plenty of opportunities for students to participate and speak up with their opinions and thoughts. He's really friendly, and his passion for teaching is evident during classes. One thing he really hates, though, is people that talk during class and disrupt other students.
sections.grading:
The grading is pretty decent, however almost everyone receives the same grade for the case discussion papers and group project, so it's important to do well in the midterm and final exam to differentiate yourself. Participating during class also helps a lot.

There are 6 case discussion papers which account for 18% of the grade, one group report which is 14% of the grade, attendance is 8%, participation is 10% and exams are 50%.

Both midterm and final exams have MC questions (around 20) as well as 2-3 calculation questions (don't mess up the calculation questions because the mean tends to be quite high).

The mean for the midterm exam was 85/100 (SD was around 12), and the mean for the final exam for 71 (SD was around 17).
sections.workload:
Workload is okay as long as you don't have free-riders in your group. The case discussion papers aren't too difficult, you only need to write max. 2 pages and answer the discussion questions provided in the syllabus. The group project is also quite simple, as it's based on identifying and solving the bottleneck of an everyday process (max. 3 pages). You also need to create a video presentation for your group project.

It is important to read all the cases before class though, especially if you want to participate during class when the professor asks case-related questions.

For revision, going through the lecture slides and case studies should be enough to gain a complete understanding of what's required for the exam.

sections.teaching: He's quite a funny person (evidence: in some of the lecture videos I heard myself laughing).  Other than that, he is very patient with answering your questions. Tip: ask him for advice (indirectly) if you want some directions in your project or if you wanna know if he's interested in your topic.
sections.grading:
I think you all have heard enough about how Ronald gives good grade.

But how do you certainly get a good grade?
1. Do your quizzes -  they come in approx every week
2. Come to class - many benefits: a. get score in your in-class tasks, b. answer/ ask questions to make him recognize you, c. there are some examples he talks about in the class but aren't featured on the ppt slides nor the Canvas pages.  Although he does upload lecture videos, some of them are editted so you may not be able to get everything jotted down if you don't go to class.
3. Submit the work on time - and remember quality of work also matters.
4. Remember that he doesn't like giving fail grades, so your only hope is to revise often because there's no way you're gonna rely on the booklet in the exam. You are gonna write notes in it beforehand.
sections.workload:
You have some quizzes, in-class tasks, a midterm, a final exam -  both of which are open book (as provided by Ronald), and then 5 case studies, each with 4 or 5 questions, and a project (video and very short paper).

Is workload that heavy? Not if you've worked out a way to cooperate with your teammates: the case studies are groupwork and you can assign one question to each of the 5 members if there are 5 questions in the assignment.  Moreover, the video is just 3 minutes or so, which means it's not very substantial.  Treat it as a vocal summary of your paper - which isn't a big deal either if you start gathering ideas earlier on.
